extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in public finance and political economy
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length treatment (Adam Smith, Wealth of Nations) analyzing public debt, funding, sinking funds, taxation, coin debasement, and their economic and social effects. Discusses historical examples and practical consequences for states and private capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability and value of annuities for lives vs perpetual annuities
rubrics_metrics.description: Annuities for lives are less convenient transferable stock than perpetual annuities because their real value diminishes from the moment granted; perpetual annuities retain nearly constant real value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why merchants (in England) prefer perpetual annuities: they can be sold with profit and remain stable. Annuities on one's own life are always sold at a loss; annuities on third persons diminish in value as they continue. The passage contrasts English merchants' demand for transferable and stable stock with the French preference for life-annuities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lenders' personal motives shape the form of government borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The differing social composition and motives of lenders (merchants vs wealthy bachelors, farmers-general, court-bankers) explain why countries adopt different forms of annuities and public borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In England, mercantile lenders seek marketable perpetual annuities; in France, many wealthy lenders have little regard for posterity and prefer annuities for lives. This social explanation affects the liquidity and stability of public debt instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borrowing facilitates war by avoiding immediate heavy taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: When ordinary government expense nearly equals ordinary revenue, borrowing allows government to meet extraordinary wartime expense without imposing immediately burdensome taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding enables raising large sums annually with the smallest possible increase of taxes; it lets governments carry on war with only moderate tax increases while deferring principal burden to future years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sinking funds are generally insufficient to extinguish war debt
rubrics_metrics.description: Sinking funds, even if dedicated, are usually inadequate to pay off the whole debt contracted during a war within any reasonably expected peaceful period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sinking funds often arise from interest reductions rather than genuine surplus; historical examples (Holland 1655, ecclesiastical state 1685) show they came from reduced interest. The text warns against expecting sinking funds to fully discharge wartime debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to misapply sinking funds during peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments commonly divert sinking funds to cover extraordinary expenses in peacetime rather than raise new taxes, because new taxes provoke immediate public complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because suspending debt payments is less immediately felt by the public than imposing new taxes, borrowing from the sinking fund becomes an obvious expedient. The more accumulated the public debt, the more certain the sinking fund will be misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual funding encourages accumulation of public debt (empirical/historical claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since adopting perpetual funding, reductions of public debt during peace have been small relative to accumulations during war; funding founded large standing debts in Great Britain from 1668 onward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives detailed historical figures for British funded/unfunded debt across wars and peaces (1697, 1714, 1722, 1739, 1748, 1763, 1764, 1775) to show that peace repayments were tiny compared to wartime borrowings; concludes it is chimerical to expect complete discharge from ordinary revenue savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding diverts existing capital into revenue (destruction of capital)
rubrics_metrics.description: When public expense is defrayed by funding, it is done by the annual destruction of some capital which previously existed — converting capital intended for productive labour into revenue supporting unproductive labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts funding with raising revenue within the year: funding withdraws portions of annual produce from productive to unproductive uses, so it destroys old capital even if it may allow private people to more easily accumulate new capital by lighter immediate taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative advantage of funding vs immediate taxation is conditional (only during war)
rubrics_metrics.description: The advantage of funding — that it hinders less the accumulation of new capital and lets private frugality repair government waste — exists primarily during war; if war expenses were met by current taxes, the public would feel the burden and wars would be shorter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that paying war expenses via immediate taxation would make war burdens more apparent, thus discouraging unnecessary wars and allowing peacetime accumulation to proceed more strongly than under funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of taxes from funding can impair accumulation in peace
rubrics_metrics.description: When funding increases tax multiplicity, it can impair private people's ability to accumulate even during peace, potentially matching the accumulation-impairing effects of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes British peace revenue was over ten million a-year and that, if free and unmortgaged, it could sustain vigorous war without new debt. But funding's associated taxes have at times made peace as burdensome to accumulation as war would be without funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment of interest is not neutral (critique of 'right hand pays the left')
rubrics_metrics.description: The argument that paying public debt interest merely transfers revenue within the country and leaves the nation no poorer is sophistry; some debt is foreign-held and even domestic creditor payments can be pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Points out foreign holders (e.g., Dutch) and that creditors are often wealthy people unlikely to be net debtors to others, so transfers can still harm national capital and productive investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landlords' ability to improve estates is sensitive to taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different land taxes and duties on necessities can reduce a landlord's revenue to the point where he cannot make or maintain necessary expensive improvements, which will lead to agricultural decline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the landlord's incentives to build/repair tenant houses and maintain drains/inclosures; heavy taxation diminishes these incentives and leads to decline in agriculture, with tenants unable to substitute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation on capital owners promotes capital flight and industry decline
rubrics_metrics.description: If taxes on necessaries reduce the purchasing power of revenue from capital, owners/employers of capital will be disposed to leave the country, causing removal of capital and decline of industry, manufactures, and commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When merchant/manufacturer capital is frequently exposed to intrusive tax collection, disposition to remove becomes actual removal; the industry of the country falls with capital removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferring revenue to remote creditors undermines local stewardship of land and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving revenue from proprietors of land and employers of capital to public creditors (who lack particular local interest or inspection) tends, in the long run, to cause neglect of land and waste or removal of capital stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creditors have a general interest in national prosperity but no specific concern for particular estates or capital parcels; their lack of inspection and local care makes the long-run maintenance of land and capital less likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical pattern: funding enfeebles states
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of funding has historically enfeebled states (Italian republics, Spain, France, United Provinces); it is unlikely to be harmless in Great Britain alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples: Genoa and Venice weakened, Spain deeply in debt before England, France languishing under debt, United Provinces enfeebled — argues funding tends to national weakness or dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even well-designed tax systems can be forced into oppressive taxation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the wisest government exhausts proper tax subjects, urgent necessity may force recourse to improper taxes, potentially making even a good system (like Britain's) as oppressive as poorer systems under repeated wars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that another expensive war begun before revenue is liberated could render Britain’s taxation as oppressive as Holland's or Spain's; prudent systems are not immune to pressure of necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public debts are rarely fairly and completely paid; liberation often via bankruptcy or pretence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once national debts reach a certain degree, there are scarce instances of fair and complete payment; liberation of public revenue commonly occurs by bankruptcy or by pretended payments (coin debasement, denomination changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States that liberation has often been disguised (e.g., raising coin denomination) and that fair open bankruptcy is less dishonourable and less hurtful to creditors than deceptive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising coin denomination and debasement as disguised bankruptcy
rubrics_metrics.description: Raising the denomination of coin (or debasing its standard) reduces the real value of debts and is a pretended payment that defrauds creditors and causes widespread economic harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives example: raising a sixpence to the denomination of a shilling would let debtors repay with about half the real value. Such measures enrich debtors at creditors' expense, subvert private fortunes, and transfer national capital from frugal creditors to prodigal debtors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical precedents of currency reduction and debt relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancient states (Romans) reduced coin weight/standard to effect large reductions of real debt, often without violent clamour; such measures were politically feasible and used as debt relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes Roman reductions of the As (from twelve ounces to two ounces, later to one and half an ounce) and ties to popular politics: poor citizens indebted to rich creditors, popular acceptance of 'new tables' or debt abolition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adulteration of coin standard as another common expedient
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations have sometimes adulterated the metallic standard of their coin (mixing greater quantity of alloy) to reduce the real value of monetary obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as an additional historical method by which states have lessened the real burden of debts, alongside raising denomination.
